parsed_answer.content: In Java, arrays are fixed-size, contiguous memory blocks that serve as the bedrock for high-performance data structures. Mastering algorithmic patterns involving arrays requires moving beyond simple iteration to understanding memory locality and time-space complexity trade-offs. The 'Two Sum' problem introduces the hash-map pattern, where we trade O(N) space for O(N) time by caching indices to avoid nested loops. 'Kadane's Algorithm' is the gold standard for the Maximum Subarray problem; it leverages dynamic programming to decide at each index whether to extend an existing subarray or start fresh, effectively reducing a cubic-time brute force to a linear O(N) scan. 'Merge Intervals' tests your ability to handle sorted data structures, requiring a greedy approach where we maintain a running 'current' interval and merge overlapping segments as we iterate. Finally, 'Trapping Rain Water' is a classic two-pointer or stack-based challenge that forces you to think about the 'bottleneck'—the minimum of the maximum heights to the left and right—to calculate the volume of water held above each index.

items: Kadane's Algorithm maintains a local maximum at each index: currentMax = Math.max(nums[i], currentMax + nums[i]). This ensures we discard negative prefixes that would only diminish future potential.
Merge Intervals relies on sorting the input by start time. Once sorted, an interval [a, b] overlaps with [c, d] if c <= b. The merged interval becomes [a, Math.max(b, d)].

Trapping Rain Water utilizes two pointers (left and right) moving inward. By keeping track of leftMax and rightMax, we can determine the water level at any point without pre-calculating auxiliary arrays, optimizing space to O(1).
In Java, remember that arrays are objects. Passing an array to a method passes the reference, but the contents are mutable. Always consider defensive copying if the array should remain immutable.

parsed_answer.content: A common production-level trap in Java is ignoring integer overflow when calculating sums in these algorithms. If you are summing values in a large array, always use 'long' for your accumulators to prevent silent overflow errors. Additionally, when dealing with 'Two Sum', ensure you handle the edge case where the same element cannot be used twice by checking the index in your Map.
